cards.b: A learned action with a specific outcome that can be improved by practice.
An inherited, stable trait that helps in learning skills.
Performed in an unpredictable environment, e.g. a hockey pass.
Performed in a predictable environment, e.g. a golf drive.
Fine: small precise movements (darts). Gross: large muscle movements (sprinting).
The brain can deal with only one decision at a time.
Beginner: thinks about each part, many errors, needs extrinsic feedback.
Practising: fewer errors, smoother movement, uses feedback.
Skill is automatic and consistent; performer can think about tactics.
From the performer's own senses (the feel).
From an external source such as a coach or video.
Information about the outcome, e.g. the score.
Specific, Measurable, Agreed, Realistic, Time-phased, Exciting, Recorded.
Performance rises with arousal up to an optimum, then falls as arousal gets too high.
Physical symptoms: sweating, fast heart rate, butterflies.

gaps.s: A skill carried out in an unpredictable environment is an ___ skill.
Feedback from the performer's own senses is ___ feedback.
Information about the outcome of a movement is knowledge of ___.
The first stage of learning is the ___ stage.
A coach holding a gymnast's arm is ___ guidance.
Motivation from rewards like trophies is ___ motivation.

short.q: Place a rugby tackle on the open–closed continuum and justify.
short.model: Open, because the opponent moves unpredictably so the tackler must make decisions.

short.q: Describe the four stages of information processing.
short.model: Input (senses take in information), decision-making (brain selects a response), output (muscles perform), feedback (information on the result).

short.q: Describe one example of visual guidance.
short.model: A coach demonstrates a skill or shows a video for the performer to copy.

short.q: Explain how a SMARTER goal could help a swimmer.
short.model: A specific timed target agreed with the coach and recorded, e.g. cut 5 seconds in 8 weeks, gives focus and motivation.

short.q: Explain why a snooker player needs lower arousal than a weightlifter.
short.model: Snooker is a fine skill needing precision and control, while weightlifting is a gross skill needing high arousal and strength.
